paragraphs: §1 — Recapitulation: the righteous and the wicked are two extremes; one is named for the extreme he attains

We have related, in the seventh bab, the statement of the one from whom we related concerning the difference of people's states in this world — that among the righteous (al-abrār) there is one who is buffeted (mulaqqan) in this world, and among the disobedient (al-ʿuṣāt) there is one who is granted ease in this world. Solomon stated this explicitly in his saying [Eccl 8:14] אֵשֶׁר יֵשׁ צַדִּיקִים אֲשֶׁר מַגִּיעַ אֲלֵיהֶם כְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָרְשָׁעִים ("that there are righteous men unto whom it happens according to the deed of the wicked"), and his saying also [Eccl 7:15] יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ ("there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness"). Of that there are many parallels in the sayings of Solomon and others.

And the author of the related statement explained the meaning of this by saying: I say that the righteous and the wicked (al-barr wa-l-fājir) are two extremes (ṭarafān), and neither of them deserves his name save by the conjunction of many things — which אלקרא (peace be upon him) mentioned in his exposition of the two words "life" and "death" found in the Torah, as has been mentioned earlier. As for the righteous one, he has attained the praiseworthy extreme of deeds; and the wicked one has also attained the blameworthy extreme of deeds, which are the opposites of those first deeds. The deeds of the righteous are those that יחזקאל (peace be upon him) described in his saying [Ezek 18:5] ואיש כי יהיה צדיק ועשה משפט וצדקה אל ההרים לא אכל ("and if a man be righteous, and do justice and righteousness, [and] eat not upon the mountains") to the end of the account, namely his saying [Ezek 18:9] בחקותי יהלך ומשפטי שמר ("he walks in my statutes and keeps my judgments"); and the deeds of the wicked are his saying [Ezek 18:10] והוליד בן פָּרִיץ שֹׁפֵךְ דָּם וְעָשָׂה אָח מֵאַחַד מֵאֵלֶּה ("and if he beget a violent son, a shedder of blood, who does to a brother any one of these things") and the rest of what he mentioned of the opposites of what was mentioned before, down to his saying [Ezek 18:13] לא יחיה את כל התועבות האלה עשה ("he shall not live; he has done all these abominations").

: The recapitulation reaches back over Babs 7–9, all of which Q ascribes to a single unnamed predecessor ("the one from whom we have related," man ḥakaynā ʿanhu) — the source whose two-extremes anthropology and thawāb/ʿiqāb eschatology Q is expounding (and largely endorsing) before adding the views of "our colleagues" and his own. The empirical datum that drives the whole bab is the prosperity-of-the-wicked / suffering-of-the-righteous problem (Eccl 8:14, 7:15) — the theodicy puzzle that worldly retribution is invoked to solve. Mulaqqan (lit. "made to meet [misfortune]," buffeted) is contrasted with munaʿʿam (granted ease/luxury). אלקרא (al-qarrāʾ, "the [scriptural] reader/scholar") is Q's honorific for the predecessor-authority whose exegesis of the Torah's "life" and "death" (the ḥayyoh yiḥyeh / mot yamut idiom worked out across this block) supplies the technical definitions of barr and fājir as the two termini of a graded scale. On the thawāb/ʿiqāb apparatus see glossary §VI.
§2 — [completing §1: the righteous may be righteous only comparatively]

And what he stated of that is corroborated [by the fact] that the צדיק may be [righteous] short of perfection — rather [righteous] by comparison to one who is above him in disobedience. Disobedience [stands in degrees], since שלמה (peace be upon him) says concerning Joab and his sons [1 Kgs 2:32] והשיב יי' את דמו על ראשו אשר פגע בשני אנשים צדיקים וטובים ממנו ("and the Lord shall return his blood upon his own head, for he fell upon two men more righteous and better than he"). So he named them צדיקים, though they were not perfect in innocence; rather each of them was [implicated] in a transgression or transgressions. For אבנר (peace be upon him) was defending the son of שאול, to establish for him the kingship contrary to what God willed; and likewise עמשא was among the party of אבשלום, who sought the life of his father. So he named them צדיקים by comparison to Joab, because they were better than he, on account of his saying ממנו ("than he"). The like of this is the saying of דוד concerning Ish-bosheth [2 Sam 4:11] אף כי אנשים רשעים הרגו את איש צדיק בביתו על משכבו ("how much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous man in his own house upon his bed").

: There is no surviving Arabic marker between the §1 preamble and the next-numbered §3; the discourse, however, plainly turns here from the definition of the two extremes (§1) to the gradation of righteousness (the ṣaddiq is sometimes "righteous" only comparatively), and Nemoy's text resumes its numbering at the next paragraph (the "two extremes that annul each other" passage) as §3. I have therefore marked this comparative-righteousness paragraph as §2, restoring the expected sequence. The point is exegetically subtle: Q's source reads the Joab/Abner/Amasa episode (1 Kgs 2:32) and the Ish-bosheth verse (2 Sam 4:11) as evidence that ṣaddiq is a relative predicate — Abner and Amasa were "righteous" only relative to Joab (the comparative mimmennu, "than he"), each in fact bearing real guilt (Abner's championing of Saul's house against the divine will; Amasa's adherence to Absalom). This relativization of the "righteous" label is what makes the intermediate case the normal case, and so motivates the whole doctrine of partial, worldly retribution to follow.
§3 — The two extremes mutually annul; transition from one to the other requires completing the new set of deeds

He said: so these two divisions are the two termini in righteousness and wickedness, and each of them is contrary to its fellow and removes it and effaces it, by reason of their mutual opposition and mutual contradiction. So if one of the people is in one of these two divisions and then is transformed from it to the other division, he does not deserve to part from the first [name] and to be realized under the second name until there remains upon him nothing of the deeds of the division from which he was transformed — [this] by his completing the deeds of the division to which he was transformed. And whenever he has not completed the deeds of the division to which he was transformed, it is because there yet remains upon him something of the name of the division from which he was transformed, and he has not completed the name of the thing to which he was transformed; for names that are sound in their meanings are conformable only to the meanings of the names that lie beneath them. So when the righteous one, deserving reward by his righteousness, then parts from his righteousness entirely by his practicing the deeds of the wicked entirely, he then deserves to part from the states of reward and to have exchanged for them the states of punishment — by reason of the [necessary] termination, in what is obligatory, between the two contraries; for he does not deserve punishment until he effaces the reward and its conditions, and likewise conversely.

: This is the mutual-exclusion thesis that governs the bab's logic: the two extreme states (full reward, full punishment) are contradictories, and a person migrates from one to the other only by completely replacing the one set of deeds with the other. Short of complete replacement, a residue of the prior state remains. This is why a mixed life cannot earn either of the two unmixed (everlasting) desserts: the residue must be cleared. The doctrine that names track the realities "beneath them" (muṭābaqat al-asmāʾ li-maʿānīhā) is the same name/named realism Q deploys elsewhere (glossary §IV); here it does eschatological work — one is not named "rewarded" or "punished" until the corresponding reality is complete.
§4 — The intermediate state: it merits neither full reward nor full punishment, but a graded intermediate

As for so long as the human being, at his parting from one of the two divisions and his passing to the other division, is in intermediate states (ḥālāt wusṭā) compounded of this division and of that division — then there is no escape from intermediacy (al-tawassuṭ), since he does not deserve the utmost of reward nor the utmost of punishment, but rather deserves, according to the measure of that intermediate rank of his, either [a desert] of mixed states that do not reach the two extremes, or that he be rewarded for the part [of his deeds that merit it]. And this [latter] is the weaker of the two statements in my view, since it is of the due of the otherworldly reward and punishment that they be everlasting and perpetual (al-sarmadiyya wa-l-dawām), because they are spiritual, not corporeal; and whatever parts from bodies has departed from time and its conditions and has become time-transcending (dahriyy). Therefore every recompense that comes to an end is from the conditions of bodies; so it is not conceivable that there be a passage from a reward to a punishment, or the reverse, save by a beginning and a ceasing — and that is remote from the otherworldly affairs.

: The crux of the intermediate-case theory, and the point on which Q's source weighs two alternatives: the mixed-life person merits either (a) a blended intermediate desert (simultaneous, attenuated pleasure-and-pain) or (b) a partial reward for the meritorious portion. Q's source rejects (b) as "the weaker," because otherworldly reward and punishment are by definition everlasting (sarmadī, dāʾim) — being spiritual, not corporeal, they are outside time (dahrī, time-transcending). A terminable recompense is therefore a mark of the corporeal/temporal order, so any "passing from reward to punishment" (which a partial-then-completed reward would require) would import a beginning-and-ending alien to the eschatological state. This metaphysical premise — everlastingness is essential to true thawāb/ʿiqāb — is the engine of the worldly-retribution doctrine: whatever is finite and dischargeable must be discharged here. (dahrī / dahriyya here is purely temporal-metaphysical — "supra-temporal," not the doxographical "Dahriyya" materialists.)
§5 — Therefore the minor residue is discharged in this world: the righteous punished, the wicked rewarded, here

He said: so I say that if the righteous one has had his righteousness breached in the part (inthalama fī birrihi al-juzʾu), then he is punished for that part with a worldly punishment (ʿiqāban dunyāʾiyyan), so that he may attain to the otherworldly rank with the reward having accrued to him complete. And likewise I say concerning the wicked one: that if he has done a part of righteousness, he is rewarded for it with a worldly reward, so that he may pass out to the otherworldly rank while he deserves the punishment complete. [This is] so that thereby may be made sound the meanings of what we find and observe of the intermingling of people's states — I mean the righteous and the wicked — in this world, and the meanings of what Solomon (peace be upon him) said concerning that, of the wicked harvesting in this world the like of the fruits of the deeds of the righteous, and likewise what touches the righteous in this world of the fruit of what the wicked do, of the prevailing of the wicked man's circumstances over the righteous man's circumstances for a time.

: The positive doctrine, stated at last: the small residue is settled in this life — the righteous person's minor sin by a worldly punishment (affliction), the wicked person's minor merit by a worldly reward (transient ease) — so that each may meet the eschaton with his dominant desert "complete" (kamulan) and "pure." This is precisely the theodicy answer to Eccl 8:14 / 7:15: the prosperity of the wicked is the payout of their slender good (so they enter Gehenna unencumbered), and the affliction of the righteous is the clearing of their slender sin (so they enter Eden unencumbered). The Bahshamī parallel is the doctrine of al-jazāʾ al-dunyāwī and the discharge of minor offenses against the backdrop of iḥbāṭ/takfīr (the cancellation of merit by sin and vice versa); see glossary §VI. Q's inthalama ("was breached, nicked") nicely figures sin as a small flaw in an otherwise sound righteousness.
§6 — This does not make the world the abode of recompense; it is only a "smudge" cleansed

He said: and this statement of ours is not a making of the world into an abode of recompense (dār al-jazāʾ), nor an abode of reward and punishment — by reason of its remoteness from that, through the cessation and perishing (al-inqiḍāʾ wa-l-fanāʾ) that do not resemble the requital of the Maker (mighty and exalted). Rather I say only that this [worldly retribution], in the slight extremities (al-aṭrāf al-yasīra), is in the position of a smudge upon the righteous one (al-laṭūkh ʿalā al-barr), which it is not its due that it should lower his rank in the hereafter — so the stingings [of affliction] in this world wash it off him, that there may be made pure for him the perfection of reward in the hereafter. And likewise the slight measure of the beneficence that the wicked one did, of that which is not his due, will not lower his punishment in the hereafter; so his requital for that is paid him in full in this world, that there may be made pure for him the punishment for his wickedness in the hereafter.

: A careful disclaimer guarding against an obvious misreading: to say that minor deserts are settled here is not to make this world the dār al-jazāʾ (abode of recompense), which it cannot be, since the world is marked by inqiḍāʾ and fanāʾ (cessation and perishing) — the very transience that §4 said disqualifies it from bearing the everlasting true requital. The controlling figure is the laṭūkh (smudge, stain): minor sin is a smudge on the righteous, washed off by the taldhīʿāt (stingings) of worldly affliction; minor merit is a discharged credit on the wicked. The point is that the world is the laundry, not the courtroom. This is the precise Karaite/Bahshamī sense of takfīr (expiation) and the cleansing-by-affliction (tamḥīṣ) motif that §§12–17 will elaborate at length.
§7 — Why total reward and punishment cannot be worldly: worldly goods are perishable and never unmixed

As for the reward and punishment for all the deeds [together], they are remote from the states of this world from two aspects. One of them: that the goods of this world do not perish [in the way otherworldly requital does not], and do not resemble the requital of the Maker (hallowed be His names) — for His reward and His gifts for beneficence transcend everything in this world, since we find nothing of the worldly goods bare and pure of a pain that entangles it, shares in it, and is conjoined to it. By way of example I say: that the human being, if he attain in food and drink to the most delectable of them, is not free of the pain of satiety and its heaviness and its burdening of the members of his body and its breeding of harms; and likewise, even if he have a pleasure in sexual intercourse, and it be in his estimation a good, yet it is the contrary of the good. And were these things real pleasures, they would not depart from the meaning of pleasure upon increase of them. And the other aspect: what attaches to the goods of this world of expiry, perishing, the human being's parting from them, and their becoming like vanishing dreams. The requital of the Maker (sublime be His majesty) and His reward do not resemble being of this [perishable] rank. So reward and punishment, in their totality, came to be otherworldly of necessity. Then, since there is observed [in the world] the slight smudge upon the righteous and the slight beneficence from the wicked, the necessity standing firm in souls and intellects compelled [the conclusion] that those smudges be washed off with a worldly washing, and that the wicked one be paid in full his slight due, which does not resemble the gifts of the hereafter, in this world.

: A two-pronged argument that total desert must be otherworldly: (1) worldly goods are never unmixed — every pleasure (food, sex) carries its conjoined pain, so the world cannot host the pure delight that true reward must be; and (2) worldly goods are perishable ("vanishing dreams," al-aḥlām al-zāʾila), whereas true requital is everlasting. Both prongs reprise the §4 metaphysics (everlastingness and purity are essential to thawāb/ʿiqāb). The conclusion is reached by an appeal to the rational necessity "standing firm in souls and intellects" (al-ḍarūra al-qāʾima fī al-nufūs wa-l-ʿuqūl) — i.e., it is a deliverance of ʿaql, not merely of revelation, that the slight residue is cleared here and the total reckoning deferred. The "no unmixed pleasure in the world" topos is a Bahshamī commonplace (the impossibility of ladhdha khāliṣa in the dār al-taklīf).
§8 — The prescribed penalties (ḥudūd) are temporal and finite; they cannot stand in for the everlasting

He said: and likewise I say that the prescribed penalties and the retribution (al-ḥudūd wa-l-qiṣāṣ al-mafrūḍa), since they were worldly, temporal, and terminable, have no extended, ample durations. So if the penalty be not carried out upon him for each one of his violations and his crimes that deserve retribution and penalties — by reason of what was concealed and hidden of them — the everlasting spiritual states do not stand in their stead; for those [spiritual states] are without time, whereas the due upon him is [precisely] the temporal, terminable thing. And neither of these two [the temporal and the everlasting] runs the course of its fellow, nor takes its place, nor conforms to the ordinances of justice. So inevitably justice must require a temporal, terminable punishment, comparable to the penalties that are obligatory upon him; for there is no rank [available] for that, after his deliverance from them [the penalties] in this world and his deliverance [hereafter] at [the time of] the spiritual states, save the intermediate rank — which is the otherworldly [one], except that it is corporeal, and it is the one we said comes at the resurrection (al-nushūr) and after the return of the spirits to their bodies. So there are paid to him the likes and the semblances of what eluded him of the penalties in this world, that his states therein may be made equal to the states of one upon whom [the penalties] were carried out, in order that justice may be set straight thereby — this, when there has not been completed for him a repentance (tawba) transferring him to pure righteousness. For if he has repented until he became a perfect righteous one, then repentance effaces what is past, as יחזקאל reported in his saying [Ezek 18:22] וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה לֹא יִזָּכְרוּ לוֹ ("and when the wicked one turns from his wickedness which he has done, they shall not be remembered against him"); and likewise conversely, in the passage from righteousness to wickedness and the like of that, with respect to what is past of good [deeds], on account of his saying also [Ezek 18:24] ובשוב צדיק מצדקתו עשה עול לא תזכרנה לו ("and when the righteous one turns from his righteousness and does iniquity, they shall not be remembered to him").

: The argument extends the §4 metaphysics to the legal penalties (ḥudūd, the prescribed punishments — stoning, the forty lashes, etc.) and to qiṣāṣ (talionic retribution). These are temporal, finite discharges; therefore they cannot be commuted into the atemporal everlasting state — like cannot stand in for unlike. Hence a person whose crime escaped human prosecution (because hidden) must still undergo a temporal punishment to satisfy justice; and the only post-mortem venue for a bodily, terminable punishment is the resurrection-body at the nushūr (the bodily resurrection treated in Bab 8) — an "intermediate, otherworldly-but-corporeal" rank distinct from the purely spiritual everlasting state. The whole apparatus is suspended, however, by tawba: full repentance effaces the past entirely (Ezek 18:22), and apostasy effaces past merit (Ezek 18:24) — the Karaite/Bahshamī doctrine of repentance (tawba, glossary §VI) overriding the bookkeeping.
§9 — If the worldly penalty was not exacted: heavenly affliction substitutes; multiple crimes settled one at a time

And this [foregoing] is [the case] when the one upon whom the worldly penalty was obligatory has not had it carried out upon him at the hands of the rulers (al-ḥukkām), and God (mighty and exalted) also does not punish him, before his parting from the world, with a heavenly punishment (ʿiqāban samāʾiyyan) commensurate with his crime and the measure of its gravity. For if that befall him in this world, it then takes the place of the carrying-out of the penalty upon him, since it is of the temporal punishments possessed of terminable durations. And this, too, is [the case] when the crime was a single one. But if there were many crimes, then the retribution in this world [falls] upon one of them, and there remains upon him, in [respect of] the rest of them, the requital of the hereafter. [It is] like a man who profaned many [Sabbaths] or killed a company of people in this world: there is dropped from him only the guilt of a single occasion or of the killing of a single man, and there remains upon him the rest of the blood and the rest of the profanations, so that he is requited for it in the hereafter — unless he be one who has been tested in his world with afflictions to the number of what he committed, each affliction substituting for [one] killing, so that he departs from the world with the punishment, the whole of it, having been dropped from him. And that is by reason of the comprehensiveness of justice (shumūl al-ʿadl), lest there be two upon whom killing is obligatory, and one of them is killed and the other not killed, [yet] they are both let off an otherworldly punishment alike. So this is what was said by the one from whom we related.

: Closing the predecessor's exposition (the "this is what the one from whom we related said" tag marks its end). The refinement: if neither the human courts (al-ḥukkām) nor a direct "heavenly" stroke (ʿiqāb samāʾī, a divinely-sent affliction) has exacted the temporal penalty in life, the otherworldly bodily resurrection settles it. For multiple capital crimes, a single execution discharges only one count; the rest carry over — unless God has sent afflictions equal in number to the crimes, each substituting for one. The driving principle is shumūl al-ʿadl (the comprehensiveness of justice): it would be unjust for two equally-guilty murderers, one executed and one not, to end up identically exempt in the hereafter — the executed one having paid a temporal price the other did not. The arithmetic of substitution (one affliction per killing) is the mechanism that keeps the divine ledger exact.
§10 — Two further views among "our colleagues"; and the rejected eternal-punishment view

And some of our colleagues (baʿḍ aṣḥābinā) said concerning that: when God (magnified be His name) knows of the disobedient one that he will repent, He tests him with calamities, for what he commits of sins and faults, bit by bit (shayʾan shayʾan), so that, when he repents and then dies upon the repentance, what he had acquired of sins will [already] have been retributed from him — [namely] what was obligatory upon him of punishment — and so the reward for the repentance will be pure for him (ṣāfiyan lahu). But as for a group of our colleagues, they allege that the punishments and the retribution in this world are only disciplines and chastisements for people (siyar wa-taʾdībāt li-l-nās), and that the real requital is only in the hereafter; and that whoever committed fornication, or killed, or profaned the Sabbath, or did other than that of what killing is obligatory for, and was then killed — whether at the hand of the ruler or otherwise — the punishment of the hereafter is not dropped from him; rather he is everlasting in the punishment, perpetually, without end (khālid fī al-ʿiqāb dāʾiman bi-lā nihāya). And the statement has already been made [earlier] that this which these [people] have said is not of that which it befits the Maker (mighty and exalted) to be described by, since it is not of the attributes of justice (ṣifāt al-ʿadl).

: Two further Karaite (aṣḥābunā) positions, and the introduction of the great adversary of the bab's second half. View (a): God, foreknowing a sinner's eventual repentance, "pre-clears" his sins by sending graduated afflictions during life (shayʾan shayʾan, piecemeal), so that at death-in-repentance the reward is "pure." View (b), by contrast — the position Q will hammer through §§18–32 — holds that worldly punishment is mere discipline (taʾdīb), settling nothing eschatologically, so that even an executed Sabbath-profaner remains eternally punished (khālid bi-lā nihāya). Q rejects (b) flatly as incompatible with divine justice (laysa min ṣifāt al-ʿadl) — the standard Muʿtazilī/Karaite axiom that God's ʿadl constrains His acts. This eternal-punishment-regardless party is most likely a predestinarian (Mujbira-aligned) or maximalist current; the dispute is the eschatological counterpart of the free-will polemic Q wages against the Mujbira elsewhere (glossary §V).
§11 — Scripture's life-for-life and talion show the penalty settles the account; the absurdity of eternal punishment for a slap

And also: we have seen Scripture saying [Lev 24:18 / Exod 21:23] נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נֶפֶשׁ ("life for life"). So if it has reported that the killing of this life was in exchange for (badal) the killing of that life, then what is the thing that remains [over]? And likewise what was mentioned after that of "eye for eye" and "hand for hand" and the rest of that. And it follows necessarily, for whoever says that [view, that the killing settles nothing], that whoever knocked out a man's tooth, or struck him a blow, or wronged him of a dāniq of silver, and then the struck one [was killed] for the striker, or the wronged one [killed] for the wronger — the punishment of the hereafter is not dropped from him, and that the one who struck him that blow, or wronged him of that dāniq, is in the punishment of the hereafter without end. And this is something that does not stand in any intellect, nor befits the Just, the Merciful. And also: we have seen Scripture saying, concerning one upon whom the discipline of beating is obligatory — namely the one who slanders and reviles — [Deut 25:3] אַרְבָּעִים יַכֶּנּוּ וְלֹא יֹסִיף ("forty [stripes] he may beat him, he shall not add"), and He said [Deut 25:3] וְנִקְלָה ("and [lest] he be dishonored")...

: The first scriptural argument against the eternal-punishment party: the lex talionis (nefesh taḥat nefesh, "life for life"; eye for eye, hand for hand) shows that the prescribed penalty is a badal (substitute/exchange) that settles the account — "what remains over?" If the executed murderer still owed an eternal punishment, the "for life" exchange would be empty. The reductio sharpens it: on the eternal-punishment view, a man who merely knocked out a tooth, gave a slap, or defrauded another of a dāniq (a tiny coin, one-sixth of a dirham) would burn forever if he died after being requited — manifestly incompatible with God as "the Just, the Merciful" (al-ʿādil al-raḥīm). The closing Deut 25:3 citation (the forty-lash limit on the slanderer, with its we-niqlah, "lest he be dishonored/degraded") begins the §12 argument that even God's limiting of disgrace shows His mercy bars limitless punishment — the sentence runs across the page-break into §12.
§12 — Even the forty-lash limit shows God spares from excess; fasting and prayer expiate, proving affliction discharges sin

[...continuing:] another [verse, lest] he see [the offender] degraded, so He was tender toward him, lest there befall him humiliation and contempt. And if He was tender toward him concerning the humiliation in this world, which is slight and transient, then all the more is He tender toward him [concerning] the hereafter — [unwilling] that he be in a punishment that does not terminate. And it is necessary that calamities, afflictions, and retribution demolish sins, and that thereby the punishment of the hereafter, or part of it, be dropped. And of what corroborates what we have said concerning that, and invalidates the statement of whoever alleged that calamities in property and in body earn no reward and diminish nothing of the punishment of the hereafter, is what God commanded us, at [the time of] repentance, of fasting and prayer (al-ṣawm wa-l-ṣalāt). And that is for the paining of the soul, so that it labors thereby and is thus refined and cleansed (tataṣaffā wa-tatanaqqā) of what has clung to it of the murkiness of acts of disobedience (kudūrat al-maʿāṣī) — since [these] make the soul murky and soil it and defile it. So when it has labored by fasting and prayer, it is cleansed and purified, and there departs from it what was in it of soil and murk; and the labor was the cause of its attaining to reward and of the dropping of punishment from it. And likewise we say also concerning calamities in property and the ailments of the body: they are only for the purging (li-l-tamḥīṣ) of what they committed, for they make the soul labor — property [purges] by grief, and ailments by pains — and they cleanse it also of the soilings of sins and their murk. Therefore we said that in calamities there is, for people, a purging of what they committed of sins, since their souls labor thereby.

: The argument from God's self-limitation (the forty-lash cap, with its concern we-niqlah, that the offender not be degraded): if God restricts even a worldly disgrace out of tenderness, a fortiori He will not impose limitless otherworldly punishment. Q then mounts the positive proof from the ritual economy: the fasting and prayer (ṣawm wa-ṣalāt) commanded at repentance exist precisely to pain the soul and so cleanse it of the "murkiness of sins" (kudūrat al-maʿāṣī) — which directly refutes the adversary's claim that bodily/material affliction "earns no reward and diminishes no punishment." The governing concept is tamḥīṣ (purging, refining): suffering (whether self-imposed ascetic labor or God-sent calamity in property or body) scours the soul. This is the bab's central spiritual mechanism, and it is staged in glossary §VI; the metallurgical metaphor it rests on is unpacked in §13.
§13 — The refining metaphor: as fire purifies gold and silver, affliction purifies the soul

And [further] corroborating what we have said: that the human being, when he is cleansed of the ailment, his mind is purer and cleaner, because the soul has had its murk depart from it through what reached it of labor by the pain of the malady. And that is the meaning of the saying of שלמה (peace be upon him) [Prov 17:3] מצרף לכסף וכור לזהב ובֹחֵן לִבּוֹת יְהוָה ("a refining-pot for silver and a furnace for gold, but the Lord is the tester of hearts") — He means by it: just as gold and silver, when they are put into the fire and there are cast upon them substances that remove from them what is in them of dross, are then refined and cleansed, so likewise God (mighty and exalted), when He wishes to refine souls and cleanse them of what is in them of murk, tests them with calamities and hardships, so that they are refined and cleansed. And that is the meaning of [Zech 13:9] וּצְרַפְתִּים כִּצְרֹף אֶת־הַכֶּסֶף וּבְחַנְתִּים כִּבְחֹן אֶת־הַזָּהָב ("and I will refine them as silver is refined, and I will test them as gold is tested"), and His saying [Mal 3:3] וְטִהַר אֶת בְּנֵי לֵוִי וְזִקַּק אֹתָם כַּזָּהָב וְכַכֶּסֶף ("and he shall purify the sons of Levi and refine them as gold and as silver").

: The metallurgical tamḥīṣ metaphor, made explicit: affliction is to the soul as the refiner's fire is to gold and silver — it burns off the dross (ghishsh) of sin. Q anchors it in the standard prooftext chain (Prov 17:3, Zech 13:9, Mal 3:3), all of which liken divine testing to metal-refining (ṣāraf, baḥan, ziqqēq). The empirical observation that opens the section — a person's mind is clearer after recovering from illness — is offered as a this-worldly confirmation that suffering scours and clarifies. The metaphor secures the doctrine's core claim against the §10/§18 adversary: suffering is not penal waste but purgative work that has eschatological cash value.
§14 — The position Q holds to be the truth: confessed capital sin, if punished by death, discharges the otherworldly penalty

And others said a statement that is the truth in our view (huwa al-ḥaqq ʿindanā) — namely that whoever commits a transgression for which killing is obligatory upon him, while he is acknowledging and confessing (muqirr muʿtarif) that he is disobedient, opposing the command of God, and is then killed for it — the punishment of the hereafter is voided (hudira) from him. And they adduced as proof for that what we have mentioned before, that the disobedient who are excessive in acts of disobedience — Scripture has reported that they may be granted ease in the abode of this world, that the punishment of the hereafter may be made pure for them. And more emphatic than that is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him), as it is [Ps 92:8] בִּפְרֹחַ רְשָׁעִים כְּמוֹ עֵשֶׂב וַיָּצִיצוּ כָּל פּוֹעֲלֵי אָוֶן לְהִשָּׁמְדָם עֲדֵי עַד ("when the wicked spring up like grass and all the workers of iniquity flourish, it is that they may be destroyed forever"). So he reported that the reason for the growth of the wicked and their luxuriance in favors (niʿam) is that they may be uprooted unto eternity; [and] the meaning of this uprooting and destruction is the descent of punishment upon them in the hereafter forever. And this is very emphatic. And the like of it is His saying [Ps 4:8] נָתַתָּה שִׂמְחָה בְלִבִּי מֵעֵת דְּגָנָם וְתִירוֹשָׁם רַבּוּ ("You have put joy in my heart, from the time their grain and their wine increased") — that is: You have gladdened me with what You bestowed upon them, since I knew that You did that to them only that the punishment of the hereafter might be made pure for them. And the like of that is His saying [Ps 73:3] כִּי קִנֵּאתִי בַּהוֹלְלִים שְׁלוֹם רְשָׁעִים אֶרְאֶה ("for I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked") to the end of the account, and his saying at the end of that [Ps 73:18] אַךְ בַּחֲלָקוֹת תָּשִׁית לָמוֹ הִפַּלְתָּם לְמַשּׁוּאוֹת ("surely You set them in slippery places, You cast them down to ruins"). So he reported that this safety and these worldly favors were appointed for them only that that might be an addition to their affliction in the hereafter.

: Q steps forward with the view he endorses: a confessed capital sinner who is executed has the otherworldly penalty voided (hudira ʿanhu, "shed/forfeited," the root hadr = blood shed with impunity, with a pointed legal resonance). The condition of confession (muqirr muʿtarif) matters — the sinner dies acknowledging guilt, so the execution is a just settlement, not mere death. The supporting move generalizes the prosperity-of-the-wicked theodicy: the favors lavished on the wicked (Ps 92:8; 4:8; 73:3, 18) are their payout in this world, securing their unmitigated punishment in the next ("that they may be destroyed forever," ʿadei ʿad). Note the attribution of Ps 92 to Moses — a traditional ascription (Ps 90–100 read as a Mosaic block in some Jewish reckonings), which Q follows.
§15 — Affliction is a mercy that expiates: "happy the man whom You chasten"

And our master Moses (peace be upon him) said [Ps 94:12] אַשְׁרֵי הַגֶּבֶר אֲשֶׁר תְּיַסְּרֶנּוּ יָּהּ … לְהַשְׁקִיט לוֹ מִימֵי רָע ("happy the man whom You chasten, O Lord, … to give him rest from the days of evil"). So he said: happy is he whom You discipline in this world with afflictions that reach him and calamities, that there may be for him thereby a purging and an expiation (tamḥīṣ wa-tarfiʾa) in the days of evil, which are the days of the punishment of the hereafter. And the parallel of that is the saying of שלמה [Prov 3:11] מוּסַר יְיָ בְּנִי אַל־תִּמְאָס ("the discipline of the Lord, my son, do not despise"), and his saying after that [Prov 3:12] כִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב יְיָ יוֹכִיחַ ("for whom the Lord loves He reproves"). So he said: do not disdain His disciplining you with calamities, for He does that, and admonishes thereby, only [to] one whom He loves; and that is, as we have said, so that there may be in it a purging for him

: The doctrine restated as consolation: affliction is a token of divine love, sent to "give rest from the days of evil" — i.e., to spare one the eschatological "days of evil" by purging sin now (tamḥīṣ wa-tarfiʾa, purging and expiation/atonement; tarfiʾa, from rafaʾa "to mend," = repair/atonement). The prooftext pair (Ps 94:12; Prov 3:11-12) reads chastisement as fatherly correction of the beloved — "whom the Lord loves He reproves." This reframes the theodicy positively: the suffering of the righteous (the Eccl 7:15 problem of §1) is not abandonment but the most intimate sign of election. The section runs on without a closing break into §16.
§16 — The chastisement of David's seed, and the rod that comforts: affliction removes otherworldly punishment

...and the dropping of the punishment of the hereafter from him. And the like of that is his saying [Ps 39:12] בְּתוֹכָחוֹת עַל עָוֹן יִסַּרְתָּ אִישׁ ("with reproofs for iniquity You chasten a man"); so he reported that in the going-away of his property, which was [Ps 39:12] חֲמוּדוֹ ("his treasure"), there was for him in that an admonition and a rebuke — and we have said that in disciplining and admonition there is purging and the dropping of the punishment of the hereafter. And He says concerning the seed of David [Ps 89:33] וּפָקַדְתִּי בְשֵׁבֶט פִּשְׁעָם ("then I will visit their transgression with the rod"); and that is after His saying [Ps 89:31] אִם יַעַזְבוּ בָנָיו תּוֹרָתִי ("if his sons forsake my Torah"). So He reported that, of His tenderness toward David and his seed and His guarding of them, [it is] that if they disobey He sends down upon them afflictions and calamities in this world, that the punishment of the hereafter may depart from them and they may be in חֶסֶד ("lovingkindness"), which is the reward, on account of His saying [Ps 89:34] וְחַסְדִּי לֹא אָפִיר מֵעִמּוֹ ("but my lovingkindness I will not break off from him"); and the parallel of His saying [Deut 7:9] שֹׁמֵר הַבְּרִית וְהַחֶסֶד ("keeping the covenant and the lovingkindness"), the meaning of which is the reward. And the like of that is His saying [2 Sam 7:14] וְהֹכַחְתִּיו בְּשֵׁבֶט אֲנָשִׁים וּבְנִגְעֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם ("and I will chasten him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the children of men"). And the like of that is His saying [Ps 23:4] שִׁבְטְךָ וּמִשְׁעַנְתֶּךָ הֵמָּה יְנַחֲמֻנִי ("Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me") — that is: the staff with which You disciplined me is what consoles me, since I knew that there was for me in that a purging and a lightening (tamḥīṣ wa-takhfīf) and the dropping of the punishment of the hereafter.

: The covenant-of-David application: even the elect dynasty is guarded by chastisement — "if his sons forsake my Torah … I will visit their transgression with the rod" (Ps 89:31-33), precisely so that the everlasting ḥesed (= reward) be preserved unbroken (89:34). Q makes the striking exegetical identification ḥesed = al-thawāb (lovingkindness = [eschatological] reward), reading Deut 7:9's "covenant and lovingkindness" the same way. The chain (Ps 39:12; 89:31-34; Deut 7:9; 2 Sam 7:14; Ps 23:4) treats every "rod/discipline" verse as a verse about expiatory worldly affliction. The rod of Ps 23:4 "comforts" because the sufferer knows it is discharging his otherworldly debt — affliction reinterpreted as collateral relief.
§17 — Even slander endured, and Israel's "double for her sins," earn reward and remit punishment

And indeed — He has even reported also that whoever hears from a person a calumny or a reviling has in that a reward. For דוד (peace be upon him) says, when שמעי made him hear [it] and slandered him [2 Sam 16:12] וְהֵשִׁיב לִי טוֹבָה תַּחַת קִלְלָתוֹ ("and [the Lord] will requite me good for his cursing"). And the Maker (sublime be His praise) says concerning the nation, at the coming of the relief [Isa 40:2] כִּי רָצְתָה עֲוֹנָהּ כִּי לָקְחָה מִיַּד יְיָ כִּפְלַיִם בְּכָל חַטֹּאתֶיהָ ("that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins"). So He reported that her iniquity was pardoned (rāṣətā ʿawonāh) only by reason of what befell her of afflictions in this world, and that thereby He forgave her. And what, in this sense, is more emphatic than His saying to the people of ישראל [Deut 8:16] לְמַעַן עַנֹּתְךָ וּלְמַעַן נַסֹּתֶךָ לְהֵיטִיבְךָ בְּאַחֲרִיתֶךָ ("in order to afflict you and to test you, to do you good in your latter end")? So He reported that what He afflicted them with of hardship and misery was only that He might do good to them in the hereafter, when they endured patiently that misery. And the like of that is His saying [Jer 2:2] זָכַרְתִּי לָךְ חֶסֶד נְעוּרַיִךְ אַהֲבַת כְּלוּלֹתָיִךְ ("I remember for you the lovingkindness of your youth, the love of your espousals"). And of this there are many parallels of what Scripture has reported, of pardon and forgiveness for sins at the time of [otherwise-due] punishment, for one upon whom afflictions have befallen in this world.

: The doctrine pushed to its limit: even passively endured insult earns reward (David's "the Lord will requite me good for [Shimei's] cursing," 2 Sam 16:12). The keystone prooftext is Isa 40:2 — Israel's iniquity is "pardoned" (nirṣetah) because she has received "double for all her sins": the exile's sufferings are the over-payment that cancels the debt. Deut 8:16 ("to afflict you … to do you good in your latter end") makes the affliction-now / reward-later structure explicit and national. This closes the constructive half of the bab: worldly suffering, patiently borne, is currency against the eschatological ledger. The §18 polemic against the deniers of this doctrine begins immediately after.
§18 — The dilemma of the two equally-guilty men: if afflicted and unafflicted fare alike, God is unjust

So if an objector should object that all of this which we have mentioned occurs only with repentance — but as for if no repentance occurs, there is no pardon, no forgiveness, and no mercy, neither by the occurrence of calamities, nor by the descent of afflictions, nor by retribution, neither killing nor other — it is said to him: what do you say concerning two men who killed, or fornicated, or profaned the Sabbath, and one of them became known and the ruler killed him, while the other was not known of, but an affliction befell him — either [death] from one who killed [him], or from other [cause], or he fell into a fire and was burned, or died of hunger, or died beneath a collapse [of rubble] — and the other had nothing of this befall him: what will be the state of the two of them in the hereafter? If he makes the two of them equal in the hereafter, he has departed from the reasonable and ascribed the Maker (exalted be His majesty) to other than justice; and if he distinguishes between the two of them in the hereafter, he comes round to our statement, and it is established that calamities, afflictions, and retribution void sins and drop the punishment of the hereafter, or part of it.

: The adversary's fallback — that worldly discharge works only if joined to repentance, not otherwise — is met by the bab's signature dilemma of the two equally-guilty men. Two men commit the same capital crime; one is executed (or dies by accident, fire, famine, collapse), the other escapes all harm. Either God treats them identically in the hereafter — which is unjust, since the afflicted one paid a price the other did not — or He distinguishes them, which concedes that worldly affliction discharges otherworldly liability. The "or part of it" hedge (aw baʿḍahu) keeps the conclusion modest: affliction may discharge the whole or only part of the otherworldly debt. This is the engine that drives §§18–22; Q will run variants of it repeatedly.
§19 — The objector's counter: then theft repaid in this world should likewise discharge — and the problem of restitution

So perhaps an opponent will oppose this statement and say: if, then, whoever killed a man and was killed for it — whether by [legal] sentence or otherwise — the punishment of the hereafter has been dropped from him, then say also that whoever wronged a man without limit, or stole from him a dirham, or a thousand dirhams, or more than that, and then twice that was taken from him, or that [property] went from him — either [taken] by a thief who stole it, or by a flood that reached him, or by a fire — the punishment of the hereafter has been dropped from him. So if you do not permit that, you have contradicted [yourselves]; and if you permit it, it is said to you: if the wronged one becomes aware of what reached him from the wronger, after the wronger was afflicted with the going-away of twice what he wronged — is it obligatory upon the wronged one to return to him his grievance [i.e., the surplus]? So if you do not require the return of that to him, you have flouted the intellects and the texts, since you have alleged that whoever stole something from me, then thieves fell upon him, or [his property] burned or drowned, would [thereby] be reckoned [as discharged] against me for what went from him. And if you require the return of that, what you set forth is contradicted; for since the punishment of the hereafter has been dropped from him, and punishment is not dropped save by the dropping of the sin, then the return [of the surplus] would not be obligatory upon him.

: The opponent now turns Q's own principle against him with a sharp case: if involuntary loss (theft, flood, fire) discharges otherworldly liability the way execution does, then a thief who himself later suffers a double loss should be cleared — but then the victim's right to restitution seems either to evaporate (unjust to the victim) or to survive (which would show the sin is not discharged, contradicting Q). This is a genuine aporia about property-wrongs (ẓulm, mukhālafa involving a creditor), as opposed to purely God-ward sins (murder qua God's command, Sabbath-profanation). Q will resolve it in §20 by distinguishing wrongs-with-a-surviving-claimant from wrongs-without. The argument is dense and the OCR clean here; the logic is a classic kalām ilzām (binding the opponent by his own premises).
§20 — Q's resolution: property-wrongs differ because the wronged party survives and must be made whole

We said, in answer to that: although we do, for the most part, measure the recompense in the hereafter against the recompense and retribution in this world, we are nevertheless compelled, in some respects, to differentiate between the two, since the matter of the hereafter cannot be conformable to the matter of this world in every respect. And what differentiates between the matter of grievances (al-ẓulāmāt) about which they asked and the rest of the other acts of disobedience is this: that the wronged one is still in being, not annulled, so that there is need to return to him what was taken from him — either to the one wronged in his own person, or to his heir to whom his property has passed. And this is not the way of the rest of the acts of disobedience, such as killing, profaning the Sabbath, and other [sins], which are only acts of disobedience toward God, and in which there is no [surviving] party with a need that it be returned to him. So whoever did one [sin] of the kind that has this character [no surviving claimant], and then a worldly punishment befell him, has been cleared — since there remained upon him nothing needing to be returned in its stead, as there is need to return to the wronged one what he was wronged of. And that is the parallel of repentance: for whoever killed, or fornicated, or profaned the Sabbath, and then repented, the punishment of the hereafter is dropped from him by repentance alone, without anything being taken from him. But it is not so with one who wrongs or steals; rather, even were he to reach the utmost that repentance can be, the punishment of the hereafter would not be dropped from him save by the return of what he wronged and stole. And this is a clear distinction (farq bayyin) that requires what we have required and forbids what we have forbidden.

: Q's resolution of the §19 aporia, and a methodologically important concession: the hereafter is measured against this world only "for the most part" (ʿalā al-amr al-aghlab) — the analogy is not exceptionless. The operative distinction is between (a) ẓulāmāt — property-wrongs with a surviving claimant (the victim or his heir), where a restitution-debt remains over and above the sin — and (b) sins purely God-ward (murder qua disobedience, Sabbath-profanation), where no human creditor survives. For class (b), worldly punishment fully clears; for class (a), even maximal repentance cannot clear the debt without restitution (radd). The parallel drawn — that repentance, like worldly affliction, settles God-ward sins "by itself" but cannot settle a property-debt — neatly dissolves the opponent's trap: the surplus must indeed be returned, because the restitution-claim is a separate matter from the sin, which the affliction has already discharged.
§21 — Even a property-wronger killed before restitution is cleared; God compensates the victim directly

Then we say: that whoever wronged [another], and an affliction befell him in which was the going-away of his life — either by killing, or drowning, or the like of that — the punishment of the hereafter is dropped from him also, even though he did not return in this world what he wronged. For the return is obligatory upon him only together with his being in the world; but when he is annulled [by death], it has become void that he should return anything, and what befell him of the affliction has removed from him the punishment of the hereafter. And the Maker (mighty and exalted) compensates the wronged one (yuʿawwiḍ al-maẓlūm) for what reached him of the wrong, just as He compensates the killed, the struck, and the ailing for what reached them of that — when they endured patiently. And that is known by what we mentioned before, of the saying of דוד (peace be upon him) [2 Sam 16:12] וְהֵשִׁיב יְיָ לִי טוֹבָה תַּחַת קִלְלָתוֹ הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה ("and the Lord will requite me good in place of his cursing this day"), together with the rest of what we have mentioned.

: The complementary case to §20: if the property-wronger dies before making restitution, the otherworldly penalty is still discharged by the death-affliction — because the restitution-obligation is conditional on the wronger's being alive in the world (maʿa wujūdihi fī al-ʿālam); death voids the possibility of radd. The victim is not thereby cheated: God Himself compensates the wronged party (yuʿawwiḍ al-maẓlūm) directly, just as He compensates the slain, the beaten, and the diseased who suffered patiently. This is the Muʿtazilī doctrine of ʿiwaḍ (divine compensation for undeserved suffering) — God owes recompense to the innocent sufferer, closing the justice-gap that the wronger's death would otherwise open.
§22 — Some are cleared of otherworldly punishment yet still owe a worldly claim: the goring ox

So if they return [to the charge] and say: if, then, whoever stole a dirham and two dirhams went from him has had the punishment of the hereafter dropped from him — and yet you have made it obligatory for the wronged one to demand the two dirhams from him — is it admissible that one from whom the punishment of the hereafter has been dropped should yet have a [worldly] retribution remaining upon him in this world? We say: we do not deny that; and we have indeed found for it parallels in Scripture — namely that there may be upon the human being no punishment in the hereafter, yet there may be obligatory upon him in this world a loss and an indemnity (khusrān wa-ighrām). And that is like one whose ox gored a man and killed him: the owner of the ox has upon him no guilt and no punishment in the hereafter, yet he has been bound to a loss in this world, namely the killing of his ox. And if a claimant claims that the killing of the ox is only so that its harm may be made safe [from recurring], we say: were that so, the slaughtering and eating of it would be permitted; but since that was not permitted, it is established that this is not the cause [of its being killed], and [that] its owner incurs the loss even though the punishment of the hereafter is dropped from him. And the like of that is His saying [Exod 21:28] סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל הַשּׁוֹר וְלֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ ("the ox shall surely be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten"), since He says concerning the owner of the ox [Exod 21:28] וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי ("but the owner of the ox is clear"). And of that there are parallels in Scripture. And like what we said concerning wrong and the stealing of property, likewise whoever slapped a person or wounded him, and then a blow or a wound befell him [the slapper/wounder] from another quarter, the punishment of the hereafter has been dropped from him; except that if the struck or wounded one demands [satisfaction of] him, the retribution is his [the victim's] right.

: The opponent's final twist: can a person be cleared of otherworldly penalty yet still owe a worldly one? Q concedes it readily (lasnā nunkir dhālik) and supplies the goring-ox case (Exod 21:28): the owner is otherworldly-"clear" (naqi) — no sin — yet suffers the worldly loss of the stoned-and-uneaten ox. Q's neat sub-argument that the ox's being stoned and inedible (rather than slaughtered for food) proves the killing is a penalty/loss, not a mere safety-measure (else its meat would be lawful), is a sharp piece of legal reasoning. The principle: otherworldly clearance and worldly liability are independent ledgers — so the §19 surplus-restitution survives without impugning the discharge of the sin.
§23 — The promise/threat objection answered: the threat carries an implicit exception, exactly as repentance shows

And they may ask, saying: has not God (exalted be His majesty) promised punishment of the hereafter to whoever disobeys Him? And when it is said "yes," they say: if that is so, then the fulfillment of what He promised is inescapable, else the report would be false. It is said to them: why do you deny that that threat had folded beneath it an exception (istithnāʾ) — namely, [that it holds] if retribution be not taken from him in this world, or an affliction do not befall him? Then we turn the question back upon them, [namely] that it be said to them: has not God promised the punishment of the hereafter to whoever disobeys God? And when they say "yes," it is said to them: what do you say concerning one who repents — does repentance drop that threat from him? And when they say "yes," it is said: then that threat is annulled! So if they say: the threat occurred only [for the case] when there is no repentance, but when there is repentance it did not occur, [and so] no falsehood occurred — it is said to them: and likewise, the threat occurred only when retribution does not occur in this world; but when the retribution occurs in this world, no falsehood occurred. The threefold scheme: (1) apostates (al-khārijīn ʿan al-dīn) — eternal punishment (Isa 66:24, the unquenched fire); (2) gross sinners within the faith (fussāq ahl al-dīn) — punished, then annihilated (Mal 3:21, "ashes underfoot" — a terminable punishment ending in extinction, not eternal torment); (3) the intermediates (al-mutawassiṭīn, the bab's titular case) — punished, then promoted to reward (Deut 32:39; 1 Sam 2:6, "He brings down to Sheol and brings up"). This is a recognizably graded eschatology (close to the Muʿtazilī manzila bayna al-manzilatayn impulse and to debates over the duration of the fāsiq's punishment); Q reports it doxographically. Note the alternative gloss on Deut 32:39 (kill-the-unbelievers / heal-the-intermediates) — a second exegetical option Q records without choosing.
§33 — Q's own verdict: he will not decide between the two intermediate-state theories; and a coda on the "grace-and-withdrawal" party

But as for us, we do not decide categorically (lasnā nabuttu) upon either of the two statements; except that the truth, in our view, does not lie outside one of the two — and we do not know which of the two it is: whether it is the joint sharing of pleasure and pain together perpetually, or the descent of punishment first and the transfer from it to reward. And of God we ask our enabling-grace (tawfīqanā) and our guidance.

And among our opponents there is a people who allege that everything in the world of safety and favors is only a bounty (tafaḍḍul) from the Maker (mighty and exalted), and that what is the contrary of that, of afflictions and calamities, is [merely] a withholding of bounty (rafʿ tafaḍḍul). So in their view it is admissible that He bestow bounty upon the unbeliever with the most magnificent and most prolonged of favors, inasmuch as that does not harm him in the [final] return (al-maʿād); and that He may withhold His bounty from the prophet, afflicting him with kinds of tribulation in this world, inasmuch as He does not compensate him for that. It is said to them: this statement — together with the intellects' adjudging it absurd — would only be admissible if, together with His withholding His bounty, He did not afflict [him] with hardships and calamities; for this [withholding alone] is the due of one who does not bestow the bounty of beneficence: that he not do ill. But as for when He has harmed and done ill, then that would be, on His part, injustice and folly (jawr wa-safah) — [which God is far above]. And now we return to the mention of the state of the soul after its parting from the body, until it is raised up and returned to the body.

: The §33 marker is explicit. Q's characteristic epochē: between the two surviving intermediate-state theories — (a) simultaneous-perpetual pleasure-and-pain, (b) prior-worldly-punishment-then-pure-reward — he declines to decide (lā nabuttu), affirming only that the truth is one of the two and praying for guidance (tawfīq). (He has earlier leaned toward (b) as "more befitting" divine mercy, §§4, 31, but stops short of a verdict.) This studied non-dogmatism on an under-determined eschatological detail is vintage Q — compare his candor about the comparative weakness of an argument in Bab 6 §3.

: A coda refuting a further opponent-party: the "pure-grace" theorists who hold that all worldly good is sheer divine tafaḍḍul (supererogatory bounty) and all worldly ill is merely its withdrawal (rafʿ tafaḍḍul) — entailing that God may lavish favor on an unbeliever and afflict a prophet with no compensation (ʿiwaḍ), so long as the final maʿād is unaffected. Q rejects this: withholding bounty is one thing (permissible — to decline to benefit), but actively afflicting the innocent without compensation would be jawr wa-safah (injustice and folly), which the divine ʿadl excludes. This reasserts the Muʿtazilī ʿiwaḍ doctrine of §21. The closing sentence (wa-l-ān narjiʿu ilā dhikr ḥāl al-nafs baʿda mufāraqatihā li-l-jism ilā an tubʿatha wa-turadda ilā al-jism) is the explicit transition to Bab 11, "On that [same topic]" (fī dhālik) — i.e., the state of the disembodied soul between death and bodily resurrection. The Bab 11 file confirms the heading and reproduces this sentence in a cleaner reading.

- The bab's place in the eschatology block, and its sources. Bab 10 is the third installment of a continuous predecessor-exposition that Q has been relaying since Bab 7 ("the one from whom we have related," man ḥakaynā ʿanhu). Bab 9 settled the two pure cases (wholly obedient → everlasting reward; wholly disobedient → everlasting punishment); Bab 10 takes up the mixed case — the person who dies neither wholly righteous nor wholly wicked. The structural seam is explicit: the bab's first line ("we have related in the seventh bab…") back-references the block, and the tail of Bab 9 (excluded here) ends precisely by promising "let us now return to the mention of al-jazāʾ al-dunyāwī and the state of one who dies neither pure in obedience nor pure in disobedience" — which is the bab heading verbatim.

- The architecture of views. Q canvasses, in order: (1) the predecessor's worldly-retribution doctrine (§§1–9); (2) "some of our colleagues" — the foreknown-repentance pre-clearing view (§10a); (3) "a group of our colleagues" — the eternal-punishment / discipline-only view that he rejects as incompatible with ʿadl (§10b), the great adversary of §§18–32; (4) "the truth in our view" — confessed-and-executed capital sin voids otherworldly penalty (§§14–17); (5) the three-classes typology of "another people" (§32); and (6) his own refusal to decide between the two surviving intermediate-state theories (§33), plus a coda against the pure-grace party (§34-material, folded into §33). The doxographical layering is dense; the reader should track whose view each section reports — Q's own commitments are flagged by ʿindanā ("in our view") and aqūlu/naqūlu in propria persona.

- The controlling doctrine: worldly retribution as laundering, not recompense. The conceptual core (§§5–7) is that the world is not the dār al-jazāʾ (the abode of recompense) — true reward and punishment are everlasting, spiritual, and unmixed, hence necessarily otherworldly (the §4/§7 metaphysics). What the world does is launder the minor residue: the laṭūkh (smudge) of slight sin on the righteous is washed off by affliction's taldhīʿāt (stingings); the slight merit of the wicked is paid out in transient ease. The mechanism is tamḥīṣ (purgative refining), figured metallurgically (the refiner's fire of Prov 17:3 / Zech 13:9 / Mal 3:3, §13). This is the theodicy answer to the prosperity-of-the-wicked / suffering-of-the-righteous problem (Eccl 8:14, 7:15) that opens the bab.

- The polemical engine: the dilemma of the equally-guilty, and the waʿīd/waʿd symmetry. Against the eternal-punishment party Q deploys two recurring weapons: (a) the two-equally-guilty-men dilemma (§§18, 27 in its 99-and-1 form) — if afflicted and unafflicted sinners fare identically, God is unjust; and (b) the threat/promise symmetry (§§23, 26) — if the waʿīd (threat) must be literally fulfilled regardless of repentance or worldly retribution, then by parity the waʿd (promise) must be fulfilled regardless of apostasy, which is absurd. Both are standard Muʿtazilī ʿadl-arguments; Q's istithnāʾ (implicit-exception) treatment of the threat (§23) is the textbook Bahshamī reply to the "God cannot break His threat" objection.

- The property-wrong refinement (§§19–22). The most legally intricate stretch. Q concedes that the world-hereafter analogy is not exceptionless (ʿalā al-amr al-aghlab, §20), and isolates property-wrongs (ẓulāmāt) — sins with a surviving human claimant — from purely God-ward sins (murder, Sabbath). For the former, worldly affliction discharges the sin but a restitution-debt (radd) survives independently (resolved via the goring-ox precedent, §22, that otherworldly clearance and worldly liability are separate ledgers); if the wronger dies first, God compensates the victim directly (ʿiwaḍ, §21). This is a genuine contribution, not mere relaying — Q is solving an aporia the opponent pressed.

- Q's reticence (§33). Characteristically, Q refuses to dogmatize on the under-determined detail (simultaneous pleasure-pain vs. sequential punishment-then-reward), affirming only that one of the two is true. He has leaned toward the sequential view as "more befitting" divine mercy (§§4, 31) but will not butt (decide categorically). The same intellectual honesty marks his admission elsewhere that a given argument is comparatively weak.
